content: The routine patient monitoring system should be utilized instead of creating parallel systems. Background data related to key populations is essential for both patient management and program monitoring. However, in many settings, consensual same-sex sexual activity, sex work, or drug use are criminalized and/or stigmatized. Collecting identifiable information linked to these behaviors from patients receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) can lead to negative consequences for both individual patients and providers delivering HIV services. These consequences may include: Data related to criminalized behaviors could be used by law enforcement officers or others to identify patients for questioning, detention, or arrest. Patients may underreport risk behaviors or avoid health services if they are aware that information on criminalized behaviors is being recorded. Patients may face discrimination from healthcare workers or other service providers based on their behavior or identity. It is important to note that human risk factors are dynamic over a person’s lifetime. For instance, individuals may have acquired HIV due to injecting drugs or engaging in unprotected sex in the past but may no longer engage in such behaviors. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that clinically useful information about risk behaviors, comorbidities, or other medications dispensed, as well as referrals for prevention services, may be documented in clinical records such as the HIV patient card. All patients should be assured that this information will remain confidential. Additionally, individual information related to key populations and criminalized behaviors should not be included in ART registers or reported to subnational or national data management units. Clinical information, such as alcohol or other drug dependence, concomitant medications (including opioid substitution therapy [OST] and hormone therapy), and sexual risk behavior, can be securely recorded in clinic records. This includes whether the patient is receiving OST or hormone therapy at the ART clinic or elsewhere, or if alcohol/substance use is a reason for non-adherence to ART. Prevention services, such as partner testing, couples counseling, preor post-exposure prophylaxis for partners of those receiving ART, targeted risk reduction, or needle and syringe programs, may be addressed and recorded on the back of the HIV patient card by counselors, clinicians, or other health workers. ART registers, which are accessible to various clinic and other staff, are difficult to keep confidential. Therefore, they are not suitable for collecting data related to key populations. Data reported to subnational and national data management units should not include key population categories or risk behaviors if this information can be linked to an individual. Instead, HIV program monitoring specific to key populations can be achieved through community-based surveys (such as integrated biological and behavioral surveys), other special surveys, or periodic reviews of clinic records by authorized personnel for program monitoring purposes. Case surveillance data, disaggregated by probable transmission route collected at diagnosis, can also be used as a proxy for key population groups to measure the impact of HIV programs on certain key populations and estimate the number and proportion of people from key populations covered at different points in the HIV care cascade. When collecting data about gender, transgender is an umbrella term for individuals whose gender identity and expression do not conform to the norms and expectations traditionally associated with the sex assigned to them at birth. This includes people who are transsexual, transgender, or otherwise non-binary. In settings where being transgender is highly stigmatized or penalized, it is acceptable to include only two categories (male or female) for gender on clinic records to increase client safety. In other settings, consideration should be given to including two questions when recording gender on clinical forms to allow for better patient management and data disaggregation by different gendered groups: 1. Current gender (check all that apply): Male, Female, Transgender male, Transgender female, Additional category (please specify). 2. Sex assigned at birth: Male, Female. Good-quality data is critical to ensure that health workers and program managers make well-informed decisions on clinical care and facility and program management. As countries scale up HIV services to implement the treat all approach and report on associated target indicators, it is essential for sites to routinely assess and ensure data quality. As adequate data quality is achieved, the information will become increasingly reliable for use in assessing and improving the quality of care. Periodic or annual patient monitoring reviews of data quality are recommended to strengthen routine patient monitoring. These reviews involve active, episodic assessments of patient monitoring data based on the generic HIV patient monitoring system. They help facilities accommodate quality reporting at different levels, including HIV patient cards, ART registers, antenatal care (ANC) and labor and delivery (L&D) registers, and HIV-exposed infant (HEI) registers. This process supports the collection of key additional indicators and integrates these reviews as a key component embedded in routine supervision activities within the patient monitoring system.
